chapters.title: Comfort in suffering and an explanation of changed plans

parts.text: Paul and Timothy greet the church and praise the Father of mercies, whose comfort enables them to comfort others. Their sufferings and consolation serve the Corinthians’ good. Severe trouble in Asia brought Paul near despair, teaching reliance on God who raises the dead. God delivered him, and the Corinthians’ prayers contribute to continuing thanksgiving.

Paul defends the sincerity of his conduct and explains that changing his travel plans did not make his message unreliable. God’s promises are confirmed in Christ, and God establishes, anoints, and seals believers with the Spirit as a pledge. Paul delayed coming to Corinth to spare them, seeking to help their joy rather than dominate their faith.

chapters.title: Forgiveness and the savor of Christ

parts.text: Paul explains that his tearful letter expressed love and sought to prevent another sorrowful visit. The punishment inflicted on the offender by the many is sufficient. They should now forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love, lest excessive sorrow overwhelm him. Paul joins their forgiveness so that Satan gains no advantage through the situation.

Although an opportunity to preach opened at Troas, Paul’s concern over Titus’s absence led him to Macedonia. He thanks God for triumph in Christ and for spreading the knowledge of Christ like a fragrance through his servants. That fragrance relates to life for some and death for others. Conscious of the responsibility, Paul distinguishes sincere speech before God from corrupting his word.

chapters.title: The Spirit’s ministry surpasses the glory of Moses

parts.text: Paul needs no external letter of recommendation to the Corinthians: they themselves are a letter of Christ, ministered through him and written by the living God’s Spirit on hearts rather than stone. His confidence and sufficiency come from God, who makes him a minister of the new testament. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

The ministry engraved on stone possessed glory, visible in Moses’ shining face, yet the enduring ministry of righteousness and the Spirit surpasses it. This hope permits plain speech. A veil remains over hearts when the old testament is read, but turning to the Lord removes it. Where his Spirit is, there is liberty, and beholding his glory transforms believers into the same image.

chapters.title: Treasure in earthen vessels and hope beyond affliction

parts.text: Receiving mercy for his ministry, Paul refuses discouragement, dishonesty, and deceitful handling of God’s word. If the gospel remains hidden, it is hidden to unbelievers whose minds the god of this world has blinded. Paul proclaims Christ as Lord and himself as their servant. The God who commanded light has shone in believers’ hearts through Christ’s glory.

This treasure is carried in earthen vessels so the power is clearly God’s. Affliction, persecution, and exposure to death do not destroy the messengers; Jesus’ life is displayed through their weakness. Faith in resurrection sustains their speech and service. Though the outward person perishes, the inward person is renewed. Present affliction prepares eternal glory as they look toward unseen, enduring things.

chapters.title: A heavenly dwelling and the ministry of reconciliation

parts.text: Paul describes longing to exchange the earthly tent for an eternal dwelling from God, with mortality swallowed up by life. The Spirit is God’s pledge of this hope. Walking by faith rather than sight, he would prefer to be absent from the body and present with the Lord. His aim is to please Christ, before whose judgment seat everyone must appear for deeds done in the body.

Christ’s love compels a life directed toward the one who died and rose for all. In Christ a person is a new creature. God reconciles through Christ and entrusts the message of reconciliation to his ambassadors. They plead with people to be reconciled to God: the sinless Christ was made sin for them so they might become God’s righteousness in him.

chapters.title: Faithful ministry and separation from uncleanness

parts.text: Paul urges the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain: now is the accepted time and day of salvation. He seeks to avoid bringing blame on the ministry, commending his service through endurance in hardship, imprisonment, labor, and want. Purity, knowledge, kindness, sincere love, truth, and God’s power accompany suffering. He describes the paradoxes of being sorrowful yet rejoicing and poor yet enriching many.

His heart is open toward them, and he asks them to respond with enlarged affection. They must not be unequally yoked with unbelievers, since righteousness and wickedness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial cannot share fellowship. As God’s temple they are called to separation from uncleanness, with his promise to receive them as sons and daughters.

chapters.title: Godly sorrow produces repentance and renewed confidence

parts.text: God’s promises call believers to cleanse flesh and spirit and grow in holiness. Paul asks the Corinthians to receive him, affirming that he has neither wronged nor defrauded them. They remain in his heart despite affliction. God comforted him amid outward conflicts and inward fears through Titus’s arrival and news of their longing, grief, and renewed zeal.

His severe letter caused temporary sorrow, but he now rejoices because that sorrow led to repentance. Godly sorrow works toward salvation, unlike worldly sorrow that brings death. Their earnest response showed diligence and a determination to put matters right. Their reception of Titus refreshed him and confirmed Paul’s confidence in them, bringing joy and restored affection.

Paul presents Macedonia’s churches as examples of generous giving despite poverty and affliction. They first gave themselves to the Lord and eagerly helped the saints. He urges Corinth to complete its own intended gift, proving love through action. Christ’s grace supplies the great example: though rich, he became poor for their enrichment. Willing gifts are accepted according to what people have, with mutual provision rather than one group’s burden as the aim.

Titus eagerly undertakes the work, accompanied by trustworthy brethren recognized by the churches. These arrangements protect the offering’s administration from blame, maintaining honesty before people as well as God. Paul asks the Corinthians to receive the messengers and demonstrate the love and readiness of which he has spoken.

chapters.title: Cheerful generosity brings thanksgiving to God

parts.text: Paul knows the Corinthians’ willingness to help the saints and has praised it to Macedonia, stirring others to action. He sends brethren ahead so the promised gift will actually be ready. This avoids embarrassment and allows the offering to be a prepared expression of generosity rather than something reluctantly extracted at the last moment.

Sparing sowing yields sparing reaping, while generous sowing yields generously. Each should give as purposed in the heart, without grudging or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver. God can supply sufficiency for good works and increase righteous fruit. This service meets needs and produces thanksgiving, glorifies God, and deepens prayerful affection between believers. Paul ends by thanking God for his unspeakable gift.

chapters.title: Spiritual authority and the Lord’s commendation

parts.text: Paul appeals through Christ’s meekness while warning those who mistake his gentleness for weakness. His warfare uses God’s powerful weapons to overthrow arguments and proud resistance to knowing God, bringing thoughts into obedience to Christ. His authority is given to build up, not destroy. Those dismissing his bodily presence should recognize that his actions when present will match his letters.

He rejects the foolish practice of measuring and praising oneself by other self-commending people. His ministry has genuinely reached Corinth within the sphere God assigned him. As their faith grows, he hopes to preach farther without boasting in another’s completed work. Boasting belongs in the Lord, whose approval matters rather than a person’s own recommendation.

chapters.title: False apostles and Paul’s costly service

parts.text: Paul fears that the Corinthians may be deceived from sincere devotion to Christ as Eve was deceived by the serpent. They too readily tolerate another Jesus, spirit, or gospel. He defends preaching to them without charge, supported by other churches, and exposes false apostles posing as Christ’s servants. Satan himself appears as an angel of light, so deceptive ministers can seem righteous.

Reluctantly answering boastful rivals in their own terms, Paul cites his Israelite ancestry and extraordinary labors. Beatings, imprisonments, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, cold, and sleeplessness accompany his continual concern for the churches. Rather than achievements of worldly strength, he boasts of weaknesses. He closes with his humiliating escape from Damascus, lowered through a window in a basket.

chapters.title: Strength in weakness and concern for Corinth

parts.text: Paul speaks of a man in Christ caught up to the third heaven and paradise, hearing words not lawful to repeat. He will not exalt himself through such revelations. A thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, keeps him from excessive pride. After three requests for its removal, the Lord answers that his grace is sufficient and strength is perfected in weakness. Paul therefore welcomes weakness for Christ’s power.

He reminds the Corinthians of the signs of an apostle shown among them and prepares a third visit without burdening them financially. He seeks them, not their possessions, and gladly spends himself for them. Defending both his and Titus’s conduct, he fears finding quarrels, pride, disorder, and unrepented sexual sin when he arrives.

chapters.title: Examine yourselves and be restored in peace

parts.text: Preparing his third visit, Paul invokes the requirement for two or three witnesses and warns that persistent wrongdoing will face correction. Christ, though crucified in weakness, lives by God’s power, and that power will be evident in Paul’s dealings with them. The Corinthians should examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith and recognize Jesus Christ within them.

Paul prays for their honest conduct and restoration rather than for his own reputation. His authority serves truth and their strengthening, so he writes beforehand to avoid severity in person. He closes by urging maturity, comfort, unity, and peace, followed by greetings and a blessing of Christ’s grace, God’s love, and the Holy Ghost’s fellowship.
